ai.literal: Even having wandered, plough behind it is, world; therefore, even having toiled, farming indeed foremost.
ai.translation: Though the world wanders through many pursuits, it ultimately follows the plough. Therefore, despite the hardship it entails, farming is the foremost profession.
ai.modern: உலகம் பல தொழில்களைச் செய்து சுழன்றாலும், அது ஏர்த்தொழிலின் பின்னாலேயே நிற்கிறது. அதனால் எவ்வளவு துன்பப்பட்டாலும் உழவுத் தொழிலே முதன்மையானது.
ai.explanation: The couplet establishes agriculture as the foundational pillar of human society. The word சுழன்றும் indicates that people may wander into countless other professions, but the world ultimately remains behind the plough (ஏர்) for its survival. Because all other work depends on the food produced by farmers, the text concludes that farming, despite the heavy toil (உழந்தும்) it requires, is the foremost (தலை) of all occupations.

words.gloss: to the people of the world

ai.literal: Ploughmen to the people of the world [are the] linchpin, bearing all those who rise unable to do that.
ai.translation: Farmers are the linchpin of the world, for they support all those who take up other work because they cannot do that.
ai.modern: உழவுத் தொழிலைச் செய்ய முடியாமல் வேறு தொழில்களைச் செய்யப் போகின்றவர் எல்லாரையும் தாங்குவதால், உழவர்களே உலகத்தவர்க்கு அச்சாணி ஆவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares farmers to the linchpin of a chariot. Just as a linchpin holds the wheels and the entire weight of the chariot, farmers support the entire world. They bear the burden of feeding all those who take up other professions because they are unable to do the hard work of farming. The word 'ஆணி' (linchpin) perfectly captures their central, indispensable role in sustaining human society.

ai.literal: Having ploughed, having eaten, those who live indeed, they live; other all, having bowed, having eaten, behind those who go.
ai.translation: Only those who live by ploughing and eating truly live. All others merely bow, eat, and follow behind.
ai.modern: நிலத்தை உழுது அதன் மூலம் கிடைக்கும் உணவை உண்டு வாழ்பவர்களே உண்மையாக வாழ்பவர்கள். மற்றவர்கள் அனைவரும் பிறரைத் தொழுது உணவு உண்டு அவர்கள் பின்னால் செல்பவர்களே ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the supreme independence and dignity of the farming life. The phrase 'உழுது உண்டு வாழ்வாரே' (those who live by ploughing and eating) highlights that farmers are the only ones who are truly self-reliant. The emphatic 'ஏ' in 'வாழ்வாரே' asserts that theirs is the only true life. In contrast, 'மற்று எல்லாம்' (all others) refers to people in other professions. They must bow ('தொழுது') to others for their livelihood, eating only by following behind ('பின் செல்பவர்') those who produce the food. Thus, agriculture is portrayed as the foundational and most honorable way of life.

ai.literal: Many umbrella shades also their own umbrella under they will see, ear of grain possessing shade-they.
ai.translation: Those who stand in the shade of the grain-ear will see the shade of many umbrellas brought under their own.
ai.modern: நெற்கதிர்களின் நிழலில் வாழும் உழவர்கள், பல அரசர்களின் குடை நிழல்களையும் தங்கள் குடையின் கீழ் அடங்கியிருப்பதாகக் காண்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the foundational role of agriculture in society. The umbrella is a traditional symbol of a king's protection and sovereignty. Farmers, who work under the shade of the grain-ears, produce the food that sustains all these kings. Therefore, the protective power of all rulers ultimately rests under the protective umbrella of the farmer.

ai.literal: Will not beg; to those who beg, something they will give without withholding, hand having worked eating nature those people.
ai.translation: Those whose nature is to eat by the labor of their own hands will never beg. Instead, they will give without holding back to those who do beg.
ai.modern: தம் கைகளால் உழைத்து உண்ணும் இயல்புடையவர்கள் பிறரிடம் சென்று யாசிக்க மாட்டார்கள்; தம்மிடம் யாசிப்பவர்களுக்கு எதையும் மறைக்காமல் கொடுப்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the self-reliance and generosity of those who live by farming. The phrase 'கை செய்து ஊண் மாலை அவர்' describes people whose very nature (மாலை, which in classical Tamil can mean 'nature' or 'habit' rather than 'evening' or 'garland') is to eat (ஊண்) by working (செய்து) with their own hands (கை). Because they produce their own sustenance, they never need to beg (இரவார்) from others. Furthermore, their hard work enables them to be generous, giving (ஈவர்) to those who ask (இரப்பார்க்கு) without hiding or withholding (கரவாது) what they have.

ai.literal: farmers / if hands fold / there is not / even desired things / we have renounced / even to those who say / standing
ai.translation: If the hands of farmers stop working, even those who claim to have renounced all desires will find they cannot endure.
ai.modern: உழவர்களின் கைகள் வேலை செய்யாமல் மடங்கிவிட்டால், ஆசைகளை எல்லாம் விட்டுவிட்டோம் என்று கூறும் துறவிகளுக்கும் உலகில் வாழும் நிலை இருக்காது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute necessity of agriculture for all human life. The phrase 'hands fold' is a vivid image for ceasing to work the land. Even ascetics who claim to have given up all worldly desires still need food to maintain their physical existence. Therefore, the spiritual and ascetic life of a society ultimately rests on the continuous labor of its farmers.

ai.literal: A toṭi measure of dust to become a kaḵcu measure if dried, handful of even manure without needing, abundantly it will yield.
ai.translation: If plowed soil is left to dry until a full measure of dust shrinks to a quarter, the field will yield abundantly without needing even a handful of manure.
ai.modern: ஒரு தொடி அளவுள்ள உழுத மண்ணானது கஃசு அளவாகக் குறையும்படி நன்றாகக் காயவிட்டால், ஒரு பிடி எருவும் தேவையில்லாமல் நிலம் மிகுதியாக விளைச்சலைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the importance of properly drying and aerating plowed soil before sowing. The poet uses two traditional weights to illustrate this: 'toṭi' (a larger measure) and 'kaḵcu' (a smaller measure, a quarter of a toṭi). If the soil is turned to dust and dried in the sun until its weight reduces from a toṭi to a kaḵcu, it becomes highly fertile. Under such well-prepared conditions, the field will yield an abundant harvest without requiring even a single handful of manure.

ai.literal: Than ploughing, is better indeed manure applying; weeded after, than watering, is better its protection.
ai.translation: Applying manure is even better than ploughing. After weeding, protecting the crop is even better than watering it.
ai.modern: நிலத்தை உழுவதை விட எரு இடுவது மிகவும் நல்லது. களை எடுத்த பிறகு, நீர் பாய்ச்சுவதை விடப் பயிரைப் பாதுகாப்பது மிகவும் நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the relative importance of different agricultural practices. It states that applying manure yields better results than merely ploughing the land. Furthermore, once the weeds have been removed, guarding the crop from pests and animals is even more crucial than watering it. The word 'கட்ட' refers to the act of weeding, emphasizing that protection ('காப்பு') is the ultimate step to ensure a good harvest.

ai.literal: Not going, owner if stays, land having sulked, like wife will feign anger.
ai.translation: If the owner stays away without visiting his field, the land will sulk and feign anger like a neglected wife.
ai.modern: நிலத்திற்கு உரியவன் அங்குச் செல்லாமல் வீட்டிலேயே தங்கியிருந்தால், அவனுடைய மனைவியைப் போல அந்த நிலமும் அவனிடம் வெறுப்புற்றுப் பிணங்கிவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet personifies agricultural land as a wife. If the farmer, who is the owner ('கிழவன்'), does not visit his field and stays away, the land will feel neglected. Just as a wife would sulk and feign anger ('ஊடி') when ignored by her husband, the land will sulk ('புலந்து') and refuse to yield crops. The poet beautifully applies the dynamics of a romantic relationship to the bond between a farmer and his land, emphasizing that constant attention is required for a good harvest.

ai.literal: "We have nothing" saying, being lazy, those who sit (acc.) if sees, land called good woman will laugh.
ai.translation: If the good woman called Earth sees those who sit idle complaining "We have nothing," she will laugh at them.
ai.modern: என்னிடம் ஒன்றும் இல்லை என்று கூறிக்கொண்டு சோம்பேறியாக உட்கார்ந்திருப்பவர்களைக் கண்டால், நிலம் என்னும் நல்லவள் அவர்களைப் பார்த்துச் சிரிப்பாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet personifies the earth as a generous, good woman. It describes her reaction to people who remain idle and complain about being destitute. If she sees them sitting lazily, saying 'we have nothing,' she will laugh at them. Her laughter implies that the earth holds abundant wealth for anyone willing to work the soil, making their idleness the true cause of their poverty.
